title: Artificial muses: Generative Artificial Intelligence Chatbots Have Risen to Human-Level Creativity
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI chatbots can produce creative output comparable to humans. The authors test a common assumption in creativity research and AI discourse: that human creativity is uniquely superior, and that chatbots mainly recombine existing text without producing genuinely original ideas. Rather than studying a classroom intervention or educational use case, the paper focuses on a basic question about the creative capabilities of generative AI systems.

The study compares responses from 100 adult human participants with responses from five generative AI chatbots (Alpa.ai, Copy.ai, ChatGPT-3, Studio.ai, and YouChat), and includes GPT-4 in follow-up analyses. All human participants were native English-speaking adults recruited via Prolific in the United States. Participants completed the Alternative Uses Test, generating as many uses as possible for five everyday objects. The same prompts were given to the chatbots, with repeated prompting used to elicit more responses. Human raters and a trained AI independently scored originality and fluency.

The main finding is that the chatbots produced ideas that were, on average, indistinguishable from human responses in originality, although GPT-4 outperformed earlier models. The paper also emphasizes that human prompting, problem definition, and selection of outputs remain essential parts of the creative process. The authors conclude that generative AI can serve as a useful assistant for idea generation, but its value depends heavily on the quality of prompts and the human task framing. The paper also notes risks and limitations such as unreliable outputs on factual tasks, the need for careful prompting, and the broader ethical concerns of misuse.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI’s GPT-based conversational language model/chatbot for generating human-like text from prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as one of five generative AI chatbots in an Alternative Uses Test (AUT) to generate ideas for everyday objects; GPT-4 was added in follow-up analyses.

findings.finding_summary: For originality in the AUT, ChatGPT (GPT-3 and GPT-4 normalized to ChatGPT) was compared with human responses across five prompts (pants, ball, tire, fork, tooth). In the main analyses, human- and AI-rated originality did not differ overall between humans and the GAIs (human-rated B=-0.21, p=.218; AI-rated B=-0.18, p=.241), and GPT-4 outperformed the other five GAIs except on ball; however, 9.4 humans on average were more creative than GPT-4 across prompts.
findings.measure: AUT originality ratings by six human raters and a trained LLM rater
findings.effect_size: Human-rated B=-0.21; AI-rated B=-0.18; fork human-vs-GAI t=2.75, d=1.15; tooth AI-rated human-vs-GAI t=3.99, d=0.65; GPT-4 follow-up not pooled into a single effect size
findings.sample_size: n=100 humans; 5 GAI chatbots (ChatGPT versions 3 and 4 included in analyses)

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic generative AI chatbot or language-model system that produces text responses from written prompts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper conceptually discusses generative AI chatbots as prompt-based assistants in creative ideation, but the empirical study actually evaluates specific products rather than an unnamed generic tool.

identified_tools.name: Alpa.ai
identified_tools.description: An open-source system for training and deploying large-scale neural networks.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as one of the evaluated GAI chatbots in the AUT; used in chatbot mode with maximum response length.

findings.finding_summary: Alpa.ai was one of five GAI chatbots compared with humans on AUT originality and fluency. It did not return any response for the pants prompt, and it was not found to be more original than the other GAIs across all prompts.
findings.sample_size: part of n=100 human participants and 5 GAIs

identified_tools.name: Copy.ai
identified_tools.description: A content-generation tool using NLP/ML to help create text such as social media posts and blogs.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as one of the evaluated GAI chatbots in the AUT; the 'freestyle' template with 'more like this' was used three times to elicit additional ideas.

findings.finding_summary: Copy.ai was one of the evaluated GAI chatbots in the AUT. The paper reports no overall superiority for Copy.ai over the other GAIs across all prompts; specific prompt-level differences were not highlighted for Copy.ai in the main text.
findings.sample_size: part of n=100 human participants and 5 GAIs

identified_tools.name: Studio.ai
identified_tools.description: AI21 Studio, a developer platform based on the Jurassic-1 language model for building applications and services.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as one of the evaluated GAI chatbots in the AUT; the Playground interface was used to interact freely.

findings.finding_summary: Studio.ai was one of the GAI chatbots compared on AUT originality and fluency. The paper reports that none of the GAIs emerged as more original than the others across all five prompts.
findings.sample_size: part of n=100 human participants and 5 GAIs

identified_tools.name: YouChat
identified_tools.description: An AI-powered search assistant and messaging platform from You.com that can answer questions, summarize content, translate text, and provide recommendations.
identified_tools.use_case: Included as one of the evaluated GAI chatbots in the AUT; used to generate alternative uses for the test objects.

findings.finding_summary: YouChat was one of the GAI chatbots compared with human respondents on AUT originality and fluency. The paper reports no overall difference among the GAIs across all five prompts.
findings.sample_size: part of n=100 human participants and 5 GAIs

quality_tier_rationale: This is a primary experimental comparison with blind ratings and quantitative analyses, but it is about creativity tasks rather than education, and the paper does not study K-12 coaching or lesson feedback. The design is clear, yet the evidence is indirect for the stated research topic.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported effects on originality are mixed and often null, with no single consistent medium-or-large impact across tools. The study suggests potential for idea generation, but the practical impact on K-12 instructional coaching or lesson-plan feedback is not demonstrated here.
